title: Markets and Trade: Where Buying Meets Selling
subject: Social Science
description: What markets are and the many forms they take, how supply and demand set prices, shortages and surpluses, fair prices, bargaining vs fixed prices vs auctions, and profit and loss — with Myra, Kreena and the canteen uncle.

questions.question: According to the chapter, what is a market?
options: Any place where buyers and sellers exchange goods or services for money
A large open ground in a village where only food items are sold
A shop that sells only toys and sports balls to young children
A building where people go to look at goods but never buy them
questions.explanation: The chapter defines a market as any place where buyers and sellers come together to exchange goods or services for money. It need not be big or sell only food.

questions.question: In a market, buyers and sellers exchange goods or services for what?
questions.explanation: The chapter says goods or services are exchanged for money in a market.

questions.question: Markets have existed for thousands of years.
questions.explanation: The chapter states that markets have existed for thousands of years, long before coins were invented.

questions.question: Markets were invented only after coins were invented.
questions.explanation: This is false. Long before coins were invented, people gathered at a fixed spot to trade goods — so markets are older than coins.

questions.question: Before coins were invented, how did people trade?
options: They used websites and apps to order goods
They waited for sellers to visit each home
They gathered at a fixed spot to trade goods
They sent letters asking for the goods they needed
questions.explanation: The chapter says people would gather at a fixed spot to trade goods long before coins existed. Websites and apps are modern markets.

questions.question: Over time, the old fixed trading spots became which of these?
questions.explanation: The chapter says those trading spots became haats, bazaars and mandis — all traditional kinds of markets.

questions.question: Why does Myra visit the markets at the start of the chapter?
options: Her ball is old and needs replacing
Her bicycle tyre has a puncture
She wants to sell cups of lemonade
She needs a new set of school books
questions.explanation: The chapter says Myra's ball is old and needs replacing, so we follow the markets she visits. Her lemonade stall appears later, in the profit section.

questions.question: Today, the chapter says markets have ALSO become which of these?
questions.explanation: Markets are no longer only physical spots like haats and mandis; today they have also become websites and apps.

questions.question: Which TWO things are needed for a market to exist, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: The heart of every market is a buyer who needs something and a seller who has it. A market does not need a large space or fixed tags.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT named in the chapter as a kind of traditional market?
questions.explanation: Haats, bazaars and mandis are the traditional trading spots named in the chapter. A classroom is not a market.

questions.question: Which statement about markets is correct?
options: Markets began with the first websites
Markets need coins in order to work
Markets exist only in large cities
The idea of a market is older than coins
questions.explanation: People traded at fixed spots long before coins were invented, so the market idea is older than coins. Markets exist in villages (haats) and online too.

questions.question: Besides goods, what else does the chapter say can be exchanged in a market?
questions.explanation: The chapter's definition says buyers and sellers exchange goods OR services for money.

questions.question: A market is any place where buyers and sellers come together.
questions.explanation: This matches the chapter's definition exactly — any place where buyers and sellers come together to exchange goods or services for money.

questions.question: Myra needs a new ball and goes to the market. In this market, Myra is the…
questions.explanation: Myra needs something (a ball) and will pay money for it, so she is the buyer. The person who has the ball to sell is the seller.

questions.question: According to the chapter, a mandi is a modern online version of a market.
questions.explanation: A mandi is one of the traditional trading spots (with haats and bazaars). The modern versions are websites and apps.

questions.question: A village haat and a shopping app are BOTH markets because…
options: Both sell only fresh vegetables and fruit
Both existed before coins were invented
Both bring buyers and sellers together
Both open only on fixed days of the week
questions.explanation: Whatever its form, a market is where a buyer who needs something meets a seller who has it. That is true of a haat and of an app.

questions.question: Which of these shows the oldest form of market described in the chapter?
options: A WhatsApp message from a vegetable seller
A supermarket with fixed price tags
A website that delivers goods to homes
People meeting at a fixed spot to swap goods
questions.explanation: Before coins, people gathered at a fixed spot to trade goods — the oldest form. WhatsApp, supermarkets and websites are much newer.

questions.question: Does a market have to be a large open space?
options: No, a small shop also counts
Yes, it must be a big open ground
Yes, unless it is a weekly haat
No, but it needs many shops
questions.explanation: The chapter says a market does not have to be a large open space; it can be a small shop, a phone screen, or even a WhatsApp message.

questions.question: Which of these does the chapter give as an example of a market?
options: A notice from the electricity office
A WhatsApp message from a vegetable seller
A letter from the school principal
A phone call from a doctor's clinic
questions.explanation: The chapter says a market can even be a WhatsApp message from a vegetable seller, because a buyer and seller meet to trade.

questions.question: A WhatsApp message from a vegetable seller cannot be a market because it is not a place.
questions.explanation: The chapter says a market CAN be a WhatsApp message from a vegetable seller. What matters is a buyer and seller coming together, not a physical place.

questions.question: No matter how markets change, what stays the same at the heart of every market?
options: A fixed shop with a price tag on every single item
A weekly day when everyone comes together to trade
A buyer who needs something and a seller who has it
A big crowd of people with plenty of noise and music
questions.explanation: The chapter says the heart of every market stays the same: a buyer who needs something and a seller who has it.

questions.question: Myra wants fresh vegetables at the lowest price, enjoys bargaining and does not mind travelling. Which market should she visit?
questions.explanation: Weekly haats allow bargaining and usually offer low prices, which suits Myra. Malls and online shops have fixed prices.

questions.question: Why is the weekly haat the best choice for someone who enjoys bargaining?
options: Haats allow bargaining and low prices
Haats have fixed price tags on goods
Haats deliver vegetables to your home
Haats are open every day of the week
questions.explanation: In weekly haats and street markets, buyers and sellers bargain. Fixed prices belong to supermarkets and online shops.

questions.question: Mumma buys vegetables from the weekly haat every Tuesday and from the kirana store on other days. Why two markets?
options: Both markets sell in exactly the same way
The haat is weekly; the kirana store is open daily
The kirana store sells only on Tuesdays
The haat is an online market she uses daily
questions.explanation: A haat happens only once a week, so on other days she needs a market that is open daily — the kirana store. Different markets serve different needs.

questions.question: Which type of market works through a phone screen?
questions.explanation: The chapter says a market can be a phone screen — that is an online market (website or app).

questions.question: The chapter asks why online markets became important during lockdown. Which reason fits best?
options: Shops gave away goods for free
Haats were open more often than before
Prices were fixed by the government
People could buy without leaving home
questions.explanation: During lockdown people could not go out to haats or shops, so markets on phone screens and websites let them buy from home.

questions.question: A market can be as small as a single shop.
questions.explanation: The chapter says a market does not have to be a large open space — it can be a small shop.

questions.question: Which TWO of these are examples of markets mentioned in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter lists a small shop, a phone screen and a WhatsApp message from a seller as markets. Playgrounds and stations are not named.

questions.question: 'Different markets help people buy and sell in different ways.' Which pair shows this best?
options: Bargaining at a haat vs fixed prices online
Buying tomatoes vs buying potatoes at a haat
Shopping in the morning vs in the evening
Paying with coins vs paying with notes
questions.explanation: Haats use bargaining while online shops use fixed prices — two different ways of buying and selling in two kinds of market.

questions.question: Checkpoint 1 asks you to read each situation and decide…
options: How much profit the seller made that day
Which market makes the most sense, and why
Whether the price is fair for both sides
Whether there is a shortage or a surplus
questions.explanation: Checkpoint 1 says: read each situation, decide which market makes the most sense, and give a reason why.

questions.question: The chapter says a large shopping mall is the only true market because it has many shops.
questions.explanation: The chapter says the opposite — a market does not have to be large; a small shop, a phone screen or a WhatsApp message can all be markets.

questions.question: You want goods brought to you without travelling anywhere. Which market fits best?
questions.explanation: Online markets work through websites and apps on a phone screen, so you can buy without travelling.

questions.question: The heart of every market is a buyer who needs something and a seller who has it.
questions.explanation: The chapter says this is what stays the same no matter how much markets change.

questions.question: A vegetable seller sends a WhatsApp message with prices and a customer orders. The chapter would call this…
options: Not a market, because no shop is involved
Not a market, because there is no bargaining
A surplus, because goods were offered
A market, because a buyer and seller meet
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly counts a WhatsApp message from a vegetable seller as a market: a buyer who needs something meets a seller who has it.

questions.question: Which feature is the SAME in a haat, a kirana store and a shopping app?
options: A buyer and a seller exchanging
Goods sold from a fixed shop
questions.explanation: All three are markets because a buyer and seller exchange goods for money. Bargaining, fixed shops and weekly timing differ between them.

questions.question: When many people want to buy something, it is called…
questions.explanation: Mama explains: when many people want something, it's called demand. Supply is when many goods are available to sell.

questions.question: When many goods are available to sell, it is called…
questions.explanation: When many goods are available to sell, it is called supply. Demand is about how many people want to buy.

questions.question: In the tomato story, why were so many people at the market?
options: The tomatoes were being given free
The seller was holding an auction
The market was open only that day
Many people wanted to buy tomatoes
questions.explanation: Mama says many people were there because many people wanted to buy tomatoes — that is demand.

questions.question: When there are enough tomatoes AND many people want them, the chapter says…
options: There is a shortage of tomatoes
There is a surplus of tomatoes
questions.explanation: Enough supply meeting plenty of demand means demand and supply are balanced — and that is when the price is fair for everyone.

questions.question: According to Mama, what decides the price?
options: The number of shops in the market
The balance of supply and demand
The government fixes it each morning
The oldest seller in the market
questions.explanation: Mama says: 'The price is decided by the balance of supply and demand.'

questions.question: When demand is high, many people want the same thing.
questions.explanation: The chapter says: when demand is high, many people want the same thing; when demand is low, fewer people want it.

questions.question: When demand is low, many people want the same thing.
questions.explanation: When demand is LOW, fewer people want it. Many people wanting the same thing is HIGH demand.

questions.question: When supply is high, there is not enough to go around.
questions.explanation: When supply is high, there is plenty for everyone. 'Not enough to go around' describes LOW supply.

questions.question: When supply is low…
options: Sellers are left with unsold goods
There is not enough to go around
questions.explanation: The chapter says when supply is low, there is not enough to go around. Unsold goods happen when supply is too high.

questions.question: When supply is high…
options: There is a shortage of goods
questions.explanation: High supply means plenty for everyone. A shortage and rising prices come with LOW supply.

questions.question: Every market, from a village haat to a global website, runs on the same idea. What is it?
options: Someone has something, someone needs it, they agree a price
The seller decides the price and buyers must accept it
Buyers pay whatever price the government has fixed
Goods are swapped without any money changing hands
questions.explanation: The chapter says every market runs on one simple idea: someone has something, someone else needs it, and they agree on a price.

questions.question: Which of these describes DEMAND, not supply?
options: Comics are piled high on shelves
Many children want the new comic
The shop has 200 comics in stock
questions.explanation: Demand is about how many people WANT to buy. Stock, extra copies and piled shelves all describe supply.

questions.question: Which of these describes SUPPLY, not demand?
options: Children ask for mangoes every day
Families queue up to buy mangoes
questions.explanation: Supply is how much is available to sell — 500 crates. Wanting, asking and queueing all describe demand.

questions.question: Select the TWO statements that are TRUE.
options: High demand means many people want the same thing
Low supply means there is not enough to go around
High supply means fewer people want the item
Low demand means there is plenty for everyone
questions.explanation: High demand = many want the same thing; low supply = not enough to go around. 'Fewer people want it' is low demand, and 'plenty for everyone' is high supply.

questions.question: The chapter says the price is 'fair for everyone' when…
options: Supply is much greater than demand
Demand is much greater than supply
The seller sets the highest price
questions.explanation: In the tomato dialogue, the price is fair for everyone when demand and supply are balanced.

questions.question: The chapter says the price in a market is decided by the seller alone.
questions.explanation: The price is decided by the balance of supply and demand, not by the seller alone.

questions.question: In the tomato story, who explains supply and demand to the child?
questions.explanation: The child asks 'Mama, why are so many people here today?' and Mama explains demand, supply and price.

questions.question: 'Fewer people want it' describes which situation?
questions.explanation: Demand is about how many people want something, so fewer people wanting it is LOW demand. Low supply means not enough goods.

questions.topic: How Supply and Demand Move Prices
questions.question: If supply goes up, prices will usually…
questions.explanation: The chapter says if supply goes up, prices usually go down because people have more choices and can look for cheaper deals.

questions.topic: How Supply and Demand Move Prices
questions.question: If supply goes down, prices will usually…
questions.explanation: If supply goes down, there is not enough for everyone who wants it (a shortage), so prices usually go up.

questions.topic: How Supply and Demand Move Prices
questions.question: Why do prices usually FALL when supply goes up?
options: People have more choices and look for cheaper deals
Sellers are forced by law to cut their prices
Buyers stop wanting the item once there is more of it
The goods become lower in quality when plentiful
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that with more supply, people have more choices and can look for cheaper deals, which pushes prices down.

questions.topic: How Supply and Demand Move Prices
questions.question: Why do prices usually RISE when supply goes down?
options: The government adds a tax on scarce goods
There is not enough for everyone who wants it
Sellers want to punish buyers who come late
People stop wanting it, so sellers charge more
questions.explanation: When supply falls there is not enough for everyone who wants it — a shortage — so prices go up.

questions.topic: How Supply and Demand Move Prices
questions.question: If supply goes up, prices will usually go up too.
questions.explanation: More supply gives buyers more choices and cheaper deals, so prices usually go DOWN when supply goes up.

questions.topic: How Supply and Demand Move Prices
questions.question: When supply goes down, there is not enough for everyone who wants it.
questions.explanation: The chapter calls this a shortage, and it is why prices usually go up when supply falls.

questions.topic: How Supply and Demand Move Prices
questions.question: Which TWO of these does the chapter say move with supply and demand?
options: The petrol in your family's car
The price of your favourite snack
The date of Diwali each year
The number of players in a cricket team
questions.explanation: The chapter lists petrol, your favourite snack and a cricket match ticket as prices that move with supply and demand every day.

questions.topic: How Supply and Demand Move Prices
questions.question: Which of these does the chapter name as a price that moves with supply and demand?
questions.explanation: The chapter says the petrol in your family's car, your favourite snack and a cricket match ticket all move with supply and demand.

questions.topic: How Supply and Demand Move Prices
questions.question: When supply is much greater than what people want to buy, what happens?
questions.explanation: When supply is much greater than demand, goods are left unsold — this is called a surplus.

questions.topic: How Supply and Demand Move Prices
questions.question: What do sellers often do when there is a surplus?
options: Drop their prices to clear the extra stock
Raise prices to make up for the loss
Stop selling until demand rises again
Move to a different market right away
questions.explanation: The chapter says that in a surplus, sellers often drop their prices to clear the extra stock.

questions.topic: How Supply and Demand Move Prices
questions.question: Sellers usually raise their prices when there is a surplus.
questions.explanation: In a surplus sellers often DROP prices to clear the extra stock. Prices rise in a shortage.

questions.topic: How Supply and Demand Move Prices
questions.question: Petrol prices rise in your city even though there is no shortage there. The chapter's hint is…
options: Supply and demand do not affect petrol
A war far away can change the price near you
Your city has run out of petrol pumps
People in your city stopped buying petrol
questions.explanation: The chapter's heading 'When a war far away changes the price near you' shows that events elsewhere can change local prices.

questions.topic: How Supply and Demand Move Prices
questions.question: Which chain of events is correct?
questions.explanation: Falling supply means not enough to go around (a shortage), so the price rises. Rising supply leads to a surplus and FALLING prices.

questions.topic: How Supply and Demand Move Prices
questions.question: Which chain of events correctly describes a surplus?
options: Supply rises → goods unsold → price rises
Supply falls → goods unsold → price drops
Demand rises → goods unsold → price drops
Supply rises → goods unsold → price drops
questions.explanation: A surplus happens when supply is much greater than demand; goods are left unsold and sellers drop prices to clear stock.

questions.topic: How Supply and Demand Move Prices
questions.question: The chapter says supply and demand shape the price of…
options: Only food items at the mandi
questions.explanation: The chapter says supply and demand shape the price of everything around you, every single day.

questions.topic: How Supply and Demand Move Prices
questions.question: Supply and demand affect only the prices of fruits and vegetables.
questions.explanation: The chapter says supply and demand shape the price of everything — petrol, snacks, cricket tickets and more.

questions.topic: How Supply and Demand Move Prices
questions.question: A toy becomes very popular so demand jumps, while supply stays the same. What will most likely happen?
questions.explanation: More people wanting the same number of toys means not enough to go around, so the price rises — the same idea as the Sports Day samosas.

questions.topic: How Supply and Demand Move Prices
questions.question: Why does the chapter mention 'cheaper deals' when talking about supply?
options: Buyers bargain only when supply is low
Online shops are always cheaper than haats
More supply lets buyers choose cheaper options
Sellers always sell cheaper on Mondays
questions.explanation: When supply goes up, people have more choices and can look for cheaper deals, which is why prices fall.

questions.question: What is a shortage?
options: More goods than people want to buy
A price that covers the seller's costs
Money left after paying all the costs
Not enough goods for everyone who wants them
questions.explanation: A shortage is when supply goes down and there is not enough for everyone who wants it.

questions.question: What is a surplus?
options: Supply is much greater than what people want to buy
Demand is much greater than the supply available
A price that works for both the buyer and the seller
Money a seller spends to run the business
questions.explanation: A surplus is when supply is much greater than what people want to buy, so goods are left unsold.

questions.question: Cold, cloudy weather has made strawberries hard to grow. What happens to supply and price?
questions.explanation: Bad weather means fewer strawberries (supply falls). With not enough to go around, the price rises.

questions.question: A concert moves from a small auditorium to a big park with many seats. What is likely for tickets?
options: Supply stays the same, price rises
Demand falls, so supply falls too
Supply of tickets rises, price likely falls
Supply of tickets falls, price likely rises
questions.explanation: More seats means more tickets available (supply up). With more choice, the ticket price is likely to fall.

questions.question: Five new ice cream shops are opening in town this summer. What is likely in the ice cream market?
questions.explanation: Five new shops add a lot of ice cream supply. More choices for buyers push prices down.

questions.question: A store stocked 100 sweaters for winter; 23 were left unsold at the end of the season. This is a…
questions.explanation: Goods left unsold because supply was more than buyers wanted is a surplus.

questions.question: Darren reaches the diner, but the restaurant has run out of strawberry ice cream. This is a…
questions.explanation: Running out means there was not enough for everyone who wanted it — a shortage.

questions.question: A new dog-walking service has four experienced walkers, but only one customer signs up. This is a…
questions.explanation: Four walkers (supply) for one customer (demand) means supply is far greater than demand — a surplus.

questions.question: Running out of strawberry ice cream at a diner is an example of a shortage.
questions.explanation: A shortage is when there is not enough for everyone who wants it — exactly what happened to Darren.

questions.question: Twenty-three sweaters left unsold at the end of winter is an example of a shortage.
questions.explanation: Unsold goods mean supply was more than demand — that is a surplus, not a shortage.

questions.question: The canteen uncle makes 50 samosas on Monday, but only 10 children buy them. What problem did he face?
questions.explanation: He made 50 but sold only 10, so 40 were left unsold — a surplus.

questions.question: On Tuesday the uncle makes only 20 samosas, but 60 children turn up. What problem did he face?
options: A loss — he spent more than he earned
questions.explanation: 60 children wanted samosas but only 20 were made, so there was not enough to go around — a shortage of 40.

questions.question: Why did the canteen uncle face a shortage on Tuesday?
options: He raised the price far too high
He cut supply based on Monday's low demand
He made more samosas than on Monday
questions.explanation: After Monday's surplus he made fewer samosas, but demand jumped to 60 — so supply was too low on Tuesday.

questions.question: Which TWO are examples of a SURPLUS?
options: 100 laddoos made for Diwali, but only 25 sold
Four dog walkers hired, but only one customer
80 children want samosas, but the canteen has 20
A cricket match ticket sells out in four minutes
questions.explanation: Unsold laddoos and idle dog walkers show supply greater than demand (surplus). Too few samosas and a sell-out show high demand/shortage.

questions.question: Which TWO are examples of a SHORTAGE?
options: Petrol prices rise because oil supply drops
Strawberry ice cream runs out at the diner
23 sweaters are left unsold after winter
Five new ice cream shops open in town
questions.explanation: A drop in oil supply and ice cream running out both mean not enough to go around (shortage). Unsold sweaters and more shops mean more supply.

questions.question: During a surplus, which of these is MOST likely?
options: Sellers raise prices as goods are rare
Goods become harder to find in shops
Sellers lower prices to clear stock
Buyers queue because goods ran out
questions.explanation: In a surplus goods are left unsold, so sellers drop prices to clear them. Queues and rare goods belong to a shortage.

questions.question: A shortage happens when…
options: Supply is more than what people want
Sellers refuse to bargain at all
Supply is less than what people want
questions.explanation: A shortage means there is not enough for everyone who wants it — supply is less than demand.

questions.question: A surplus often leads sellers to drop their prices.
questions.explanation: The chapter says when there is a surplus, sellers often drop their prices to clear the extra stock.

questions.question: Which word describes 'there is not enough to go around'?
questions.explanation: 'Not enough to go around' is the chapter's description of low supply — a shortage.

questions.question: A cricket match ticket selling out in four minutes shows a surplus of tickets.
questions.explanation: Selling out fast shows very high demand and not enough tickets for everyone — the opposite of a surplus.

questions.question: In which city is Asia's largest fruit and vegetable market?
questions.explanation: The chapter says Asia's largest fruit and vegetable market, Azadpur Mandi, is in Delhi.

questions.question: What is the name of Asia's largest fruit and vegetable market?
questions.explanation: Azadpur Mandi in Delhi is named in the chapter as Asia's largest fruit and vegetable market.

questions.question: How much produce does Azadpur Mandi receive on a single day?
questions.explanation: The chapter says Azadpur Mandi receives over 10,000 tonnes of produce from farms across India on a single day.

questions.question: Azadpur Mandi receives produce from farms across India.
questions.explanation: The chapter says it receives over 10,000 tonnes a day from farms across India.

questions.question: Azadpur Mandi is Asia's largest grain market.
questions.explanation: Azadpur Mandi is Asia's largest FRUIT AND VEGETABLE market, not a grain market.

questions.question: In peak mango season, how much do mangoes cost in the chapter's example?
questions.explanation: In peak mango season mangoes cost ₹40/kg; three months later the imported ones cost ₹120/kg.

questions.question: Three months after peak season, how much do the imported mangoes cost?
questions.explanation: Three months after peak season the same mangoes cost ₹120/kg, because they are now imported.

questions.question: Why are mangoes so much costlier three months after the peak season?
options: The government fixes a higher price
They are imported, as local supply is low
Farmers hold an auction to sell them
questions.explanation: Out of season, local supply is low and mangoes must be imported from another country, so the price rises to ₹120/kg.

questions.question: Mangoes cost ₹40/kg in peak season and ₹120/kg off-season. The off-season price is how many times the peak price?
questions.explanation: ₹120 ÷ ₹40 = 3, so the off-season price is three times the peak-season price.

questions.question: If you were a mango farmer in peak season, how might you feel?
options: Mixed: lots to sell, but a low price per kg
Only happy: prices are at their highest
Only worried: there are no mangoes to sell
Neither: prices never change in mango season
questions.explanation: In peak season there is plenty to sell, but high supply pushes the price down to ₹40/kg — so a farmer could feel both happy and worried.

questions.question: Why is buying local and seasonal vegetables good for the family budget?
options: Local vegetables are sold only by auction
Supply is high in season, so prices are lower
Shops give seasonal items away for free
questions.explanation: In season, local supply is high and prices fall (like ₹40/kg mangoes). Out of season, imported goods cost far more.

questions.question: Why is buying local and seasonal vegetables good for the environment?
options: Seasonal goods never produce any waste
Imported goods are grown in laboratories
Less transport is needed than for imported goods
Local vegetables grow without any water
questions.explanation: Local produce does not have to be transported from another country, so less fuel is used than for imported goods.

questions.question: Petrol prices in your city can rise even when there is no petrol shortage in your city.
questions.explanation: The chapter asks exactly this and hints that 'a war far away' can change the price near you.

questions.question: 'When a war far away changes the price near you' shows that…
options: Prices depend only on local shops
Petrol is not affected by supply
Markets around the world are connected
questions.explanation: Events far away can change supply, and that moves prices near you — markets are connected.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT true about Azadpur Mandi?
options: It is a website that sells vegetables
It is located in the city of Delhi
It is Asia's largest for fruit and vegetables
It receives over 10,000 tonnes a day
questions.explanation: Azadpur Mandi is a physical mandi in Delhi, not a website. The other three statements come straight from the chapter.

questions.question: Which TWO statements about mangoes are TRUE according to the chapter?
options: The peak-season price is ₹40 per kg
The off-season price is ₹40 per kg
questions.explanation: Peak season: ₹40/kg, local. Three months later: ₹120/kg, imported from another country.

questions.question: In the mango example, what changes along with the price after three months?
options: The mangoes are now given away free
The mangoes are now sold by auction
The mangoes are now sold on WhatsApp
questions.explanation: After peak season the same mangoes are imported from another country, which is why the price jumps to ₹120/kg.

questions.question: A fair price is one that…
options: Is the highest the seller can charge
Is fixed by the owner of the market
Works for both the buyer and the seller
Is the lowest possible for the buyer
questions.explanation: The chapter says a fair price works for both sides — affordable for the buyer and covering costs for the seller.

questions.question: For the BUYER, a fair price is…
options: Always lower than the cost of making it
Decided by bargaining at every shop
The same in every market in India
questions.explanation: For the buyer, a fair price is affordable and worth the money.

questions.question: For the SELLER, a fair price…
options: Covers costs and leaves some extra for hard work
Is as high as possible so no one can buy
Is the lowest so that buyers are always happy
Equals exactly the cost of making the item
questions.explanation: For the seller, a fair price covers the cost of making the item and leaves some extra money for their hard work.

questions.question: What happens when a price is too HIGH?
options: The seller makes more profit every day
The buyer walks away and goods stay unsold
The buyer is happy but the seller loses money
Both sides are happy and the market works
questions.explanation: When a price is too high, the buyer walks away and the seller is left with unsold goods that might spoil. The seller loses.

questions.question: When a price is too high, who does the chapter say loses?
questions.explanation: With a too-high price the buyer simply walks away; the seller is left with unsold goods and loses. 'Both lose' is for a too-LOW price.

questions.question: What happens when a price is too LOW?
options: Seller happy today, but the buyer loses money
Both sides are happy for years to come
The seller makes extra money for hard work
Buyer happy today, but the seller loses money
questions.explanation: When a price is too low the buyer is happy today, but the seller loses money and eventually cannot stay in business.

questions.question: In the long run, when prices are too low…
options: The seller closes down and the buyer has nowhere to shop
The seller grows and opens more shops nearby
The buyer stops shopping because prices are too high
The government opens a new market for the buyers
questions.explanation: A seller losing money eventually cannot afford to stay in business and closes down — then the buyer has nowhere left to shop.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say 'Both lose in the end' when a price is too low?
options: Goods spoil because nobody can afford them
The seller closes, so the buyer loses a place to shop
The buyer pays more than the item is worth
The seller earns too much and buyers get angry
questions.explanation: The seller loses money and closes down; tomorrow the buyer has nowhere left to shop. So both lose.

questions.question: A market only works when both sides are happy.
questions.explanation: This is the chapter's conclusion on fair prices: a market only works when both the buyer and the seller are happy.

questions.question: When a price is too low, only the seller loses in the end.
questions.explanation: The seller loses money and closes down, and then the buyer has nowhere to shop — both lose in the end.

questions.question: When a price is too high, unsold goods might spoil or become useless.
questions.explanation: The chapter says a too-high price leaves the seller with unsold goods that might spoil or become useless.

questions.question: Ved says a fair price is 'the lowest possible price for the buyer.' Myra says it 'works for both buyer and seller.' Who matches the chapter?
options: Both, because any price can be called fair
Neither, because fair prices do not exist
Myra, because the seller must cover costs too
Ved, because buyers should always pay the least
questions.explanation: The chapter defines a fair price as one that works for both sides. The lowest possible price would make the seller lose money and close down.

questions.question: A seller who prices goods too low will eventually…
options: Attract so many buyers that profits soar
Create a shortage in the whole market
Be forced by buyers to raise prices
Not be able to continue the business
questions.explanation: Too-low prices mean the seller loses money and cannot afford to stay in business, so the shop closes down.

questions.question: Which of these is a sign that a price is TOO HIGH?
options: Buyers are happy but the seller loses money
The seller cannot afford to stay in business
Both buyer and seller go home happy
questions.explanation: When the price is too high the buyer walks away. The other options describe a too-low price or a fair price.

questions.question: Select the TWO features of a fair price for a SELLER.
options: It covers the cost of making the item
It leaves some extra money for hard work
It is the lowest price any buyer will offer
It is affordable and worth the money
questions.explanation: For the seller a fair price covers costs and leaves extra for hard work. 'Affordable and worth the money' is the BUYER's side.

questions.question: Which statement about fair prices is FALSE?
options: A fair price works for both sides
A fair price always favours the buyer
A fair price is affordable for the buyer
A fair price covers the seller's costs
questions.explanation: A fair price works for BOTH sides; it does not favour only the buyer. The other three statements are from the chapter.

questions.question: A very low price is always a fair price because the buyer saves money.
questions.explanation: A fair price must also cover the seller's costs. A too-low price makes the seller lose money, and eventually both lose.

questions.question: 'Tomorrow, the buyer has nowhere left to shop.' This happens after…
options: Supply rose and goods were left unsold
Demand rose and prices went up
Prices were too low and the seller closed down
Prices were too high and buyers walked away
questions.explanation: This line comes from the too-LOW price case: the seller loses money, closes down, and the buyer has nowhere to shop.

questions.question: What does the chapter mean by a price being 'affordable' for the buyer?
options: The seller makes extra money from it
The price is higher than the item's real worth
The price covers the cost of making the item
The buyer can pay it and it is worth the money
questions.explanation: For the buyer, a fair price is affordable and worth the money. Covering costs is the seller's side.

questions.question: For the seller, a fair price covers the cost of making the item.
questions.explanation: The chapter says a fair price covers the seller's cost of making the item and leaves some extra for their hard work.

questions.question: How do buyers and sellers agree on a price at weekly haats and street markets?
questions.explanation: In weekly haats and street markets, buyers and sellers bargain until they find a number both accept.

questions.question: In supermarkets and online shops, prices are…
questions.explanation: In supermarkets and online shops prices are fixed — there is no bargaining; the price on the tag is final.

questions.question: In bargaining, the seller starts with a ___ price and the buyer offers a ___ one.
questions.explanation: The seller starts with a high price and the buyer offers a lower one; they go back and forth to meet in the middle.

questions.question: How does bargaining end?
options: When the seller's first price is accepted
When the buyer's first offer is accepted
When the highest bidder wins the item
When both accept a number they agree on
questions.explanation: Bargaining goes back and forth until the buyer and seller find a number they both accept. The highest bidder winning is an auction.

questions.question: In a supermarket, the price on the tag is final.
questions.explanation: Supermarkets and online shops use fixed prices — there is no bargaining and the tag price is final.

questions.question: Bargaining is common in supermarkets and online shops.
questions.explanation: Bargaining happens in weekly haats and street markets. Supermarkets and online shops have fixed prices.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about bargaining compared with fixed prices?
options: Neither way is better; it depends on the market
Bargaining is always better for the buyer
Fixed prices are always fairer for everyone
Bargaining should be used in every market
questions.explanation: The chapter says neither way is better than the other; the right approach depends on the kind of market you are visiting.

questions.question: What is the THIRD way to agree on a price, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: After bargaining and fixed prices, the chapter introduces a third way: an auction, like the IPL player auction.

questions.question: In the IPL auction, who competes against each other?
questions.explanation: Different team owners compete by shouting higher and higher bids for a player.

questions.question: In the IPL auction, who gets the player?
options: The team with the lowest bid
The team that offers the most money
questions.explanation: The team that offers the most money (the highest bid) gets the player.

questions.question: What are the higher and higher amounts of money shouted in an auction called?
questions.explanation: Team owners shout out higher and higher amounts of money, called bids.

questions.question: In the IPL auction, the player sets his own price.
questions.explanation: The chapter says the player doesn't set the price and neither does a supermarket — competing team owners' bids set it.

questions.question: In an IPL auction, the price is set by…
questions.explanation: Neither the player nor a tag sets the price; team owners compete with bids and the highest one wins.

questions.question: You are selling old comics at a school fun-fair and want the person who pays the MOST to get them. Which method?
questions.explanation: An auction lets buyers compete with bids, and the highest bidder wins — just like the IPL.

questions.question: You want every comic to sell at exactly the price you decide, with no discussion. Which method?
questions.explanation: A fixed price means the price on the tag is final, with no bargaining or bidding.

questions.question: Which way of agreeing on a price involves 'going back and forth'?
questions.explanation: In bargaining the seller starts high, the buyer offers lower, and they go back and forth until they agree.

questions.question: Which TWO places use bargaining, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: Bargaining happens in weekly haats and street markets; supermarkets and online shops use fixed prices.

questions.question: Which TWO places use fixed prices, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: Supermarkets and online shops have fixed prices. Haats use bargaining and the IPL uses bids.

questions.question: An auction is to 'the highest bid wins' as bargaining is to…
options: The buyer alone fixes the price
Both sides meet at a number they accept
The price on the tag is final
The seller alone fixes the price
questions.explanation: Bargaining ends when buyer and seller find a number both accept. A final tag price is fixed pricing.

questions.question: The chapter says bargaining is always the better way to agree on a price.
questions.explanation: The chapter says neither bargaining nor fixed prices is better; it depends on the kind of market.

questions.question: Which cricket league does the chapter use to explain auctions?
questions.explanation: The chapter explains auctions through how teams buy players in the IPL (Indian Premier League).

questions.question: How much money did Myra make from selling lemonade?
questions.explanation: The chapter says Myra made ₹90 from lemonade — but she did not stop there; she asked three questions.

questions.question: What is profit, according to the chapter?
options: What is left after costs are covered
All the money received from selling
Goods left unsold at the end
questions.explanation: Profit is what's left after costs. All money received is income; money spent is expenditure.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the three questions every seller asks at the end of the day?
options: Did I bargain enough with buyers?
Did I cover all my costs?
questions.explanation: The three questions are: Did I cover all my costs? Did I make a profit? Could I have done better?

questions.question: Which question does the chapter call the MOST important?
options: Did I cover all my costs?
questions.explanation: The chapter says the third question — 'Could I have done better?' — is the most important.

questions.question: Why is 'Could I have done better?' the most important question?
options: It tells the seller exactly how much was earned
It shows whether all costs were covered today
It helps the seller raise the price right away
Profit is about making better decisions tomorrow
questions.explanation: The chapter says profit is not just about today; it is about making better decisions tomorrow.

questions.question: Profit is not just about today; it is about making better decisions tomorrow.
questions.explanation: This is the chapter's exact point about why 'Could I have done better?' matters most.

questions.question: Income, expenditure and profit are the result of…
options: Only the weather on market day
The number of coins buyers carry
questions.explanation: The chapter says they are the result of every choice a seller makes — what to buy, how much to make, what price to charge, which market to sell in.

questions.question: Which TWO choices does the chapter list as affecting a seller's profit?
options: Which colour to paint the shop
questions.explanation: The chapter lists: what to buy, how much to make, what price to charge, and which market to sell in.

questions.question: Which TWO are seller choices named in the chapter?
options: Which day of the week it is
questions.explanation: How much to make and which market to sell in are among the choices that shape income, expenditure and profit.

questions.question: Kreena spent ₹100 making lemonade and sold 30 cups at ₹6 each. What did she make?
Kreena sold 30 cups of lemonade at ₹6 each. What was her INCOME?
questions.explanation: Income is the money received from selling: 30 × ₹6 = ₹180. Her cost of ₹100 is expenditure, and ₹80 is the profit.

questions.question: If Kreena had sold only 15 cups at ₹6 each, with the same ₹100 cost, what would the result be?
questions.explanation: Income = 15 × ₹6 = ₹90. Costs were ₹100, so ₹90 − ₹100 = −₹10, a loss of ₹10.

questions.question: Profit is what's left after…
questions.explanation: The chapter's summary says: 'Profit is what's left after costs.'

questions.question: If expenditure is more than income, the seller has made a profit.
questions.explanation: Profit is when income is MORE than expenditure. If expenditure is higher, the seller has made a loss.

questions.question: Why should a seller know the cost of making a product?
options: To know how many buyers will come
To set a price that covers costs and earns profit
To make sure the price is the lowest in town
To decide which buyer to serve first
questions.explanation: Only by knowing costs can a seller answer 'Did I cover all my costs?' and set a fair price that leaves some profit.

questions.question: Who does the chapter say asks the three end-of-day questions?
options: Only buyers at the weekly haat
Every seller, from a canteen uncle to a factory owner
Only the owners of large factories
questions.explanation: The chapter says every seller — from a canteen uncle to the owner of a large factory — asks these questions.

questions.question: Puja sold more lemonade than Zayed. Which reason best fits the chapter's ideas?
options: She did not count her costs at all
She charged more than any buyer would pay
She made lemonade without any expenditure
She made better choices about price, place or quantity
questions.explanation: The chapter says results come from every choice a seller makes — what price to charge, how much to make, which market to sell in.

questions.question: Profit helps a seller grow and do better tomorrow.
questions.explanation: The chapter's summary says profit helps a seller grow and do better tomorrow.

questions.question: Myra 'made ₹90 from lemonade' and then asked 'Did I cover all my costs?' The ₹90 is best called her…
questions.explanation: ₹90 is the money received from selling — income. Only after subtracting costs does she know whether there is a profit.

questions.question: Kreena's lemonade stall made a loss of ₹20.
questions.explanation: Kreena earned ₹180 (30 × ₹6) and spent ₹100, so she made a PROFIT of ₹80.

questions.question: A seller covers all costs exactly but has nothing left over. What is the result?
questions.explanation: Profit is what is left after costs. If nothing is left, there is no profit — but no loss either (break-even).

questions.question: 'Supply' means…
options: When income is more than expenditure
How much of a good is available to buy
How many people want to buy something
questions.explanation: Supply (C) is how much of a good is available to buy. Demand is how many people want it.

questions.question: 'Demand' means…
options: How much of a good is available to buy
Money spent to run a business
When supply is greater than demand
How many people want to buy something
questions.explanation: Demand (E) is how many people want to buy something.

questions.question: 'Income' means…
options: Money received from selling goods or services
Money spent to buy goods or run a business
When income is more than expenditure
When supply is greater than demand
questions.explanation: Income (F) is money received from selling goods or services. Money spent is expenditure.

questions.question: 'Expenditure' means…
options: When supply is greater than demand
Money spent to buy goods or run a business
Money received from selling goods or services
How much of a good is available to buy
questions.explanation: Expenditure (A) is money spent to buy goods or run a business.

questions.question: 'Profit' means…
options: Money spent to run a business
How many people want to buy something
When income is more than expenditure
When supply is greater than demand
questions.explanation: Profit (D) is when income is more than expenditure. Supply greater than demand is a surplus.

questions.question: 'Surplus' means…
options: When income is more than expenditure
How much of a good is available to buy
When supply is greater than demand
questions.explanation: Surplus (B) is when supply is greater than demand, so goods are left unsold.

questions.question: Which word matches 'Money spent to buy goods or run a business'?
questions.explanation: Expenditure is money spent; income is money received; profit is what's left.

questions.question: Which word matches 'Money received from selling goods or services'?
questions.explanation: Income is money received from selling. Profit is only what remains after expenditure is subtracted.

questions.question: Which term is the OPPOSITE of surplus?
questions.explanation: A surplus is too much supply (goods unsold); a shortage is too little supply (not enough to go around).

questions.question: Which pair is matched WRONGLY?
options: Supply — how much is available to buy
Demand — how many want to buy
Profit — money spent to run a business
questions.explanation: Money spent to run a business is EXPENDITURE. Profit is when income is more than expenditure.

questions.question: Profit is when expenditure is more than income.
questions.explanation: Profit is when INCOME is more than expenditure. The other way round is a loss.

questions.question: Surplus is when supply is greater than demand.
questions.explanation: This is the chapter's matching definition of surplus.

questions.question: Which TWO terms are about MONEY rather than goods?
questions.explanation: Income (money received) and expenditure (money spent) are about money. Supply and surplus describe amounts of goods.

questions.question: Which TWO terms describe amounts of GOODS or BUYERS rather than money?
questions.explanation: Supply is how much of a good is available; demand is how many people want it. Income and profit are money.

questions.question: Profit can be worked out as…
questions.explanation: Profit is when income is more than expenditure — so profit = income − expenditure.

questions.question: Demand describes how much of a good is available to buy.
questions.explanation: How much is available to buy is SUPPLY. Demand is how many people want to buy something.

questions.question: A seller's income is ₹500 and expenditure is ₹350. What is the profit?
questions.explanation: Profit = income − expenditure = ₹500 − ₹350 = ₹150.

questions.question: The canteen makes 60 samosas daily. On Sports Day, 90 children want samosas instead of the usual 30. What happens to the price?
options: Price will stay the same because supply has not changed
Price will fall because the canteen uncle is generous
Price will rise because demand has gone up
Price will fall because more children are buying
questions.explanation: Demand jumped from 30 to 90 while supply stayed at 60, so there is not enough to go around and the price rises.

questions.question: On Sports Day, 90 children want samosas but only 60 are made. How big is the shortage?
questions.explanation: 90 wanted − 60 made = 30 children will not get a samosa — a shortage of 30.

questions.question: Usual samosa demand is 30; on Sports Day it is 90. Demand grew how many times?
questions.explanation: 90 ÷ 30 = 3, so demand tripled on Sports Day.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a SURPLUS?
options: A cricket match ticket sells out in four minutes
100 laddoos made for Diwali but only 25 sold
80 children want samosas but the canteen has 20
Petrol prices rise because oil supply drops
questions.explanation: 75 unsold laddoos means supply was far greater than demand — a surplus. The other three show shortages or high demand.

questions.question: In the Diwali laddoo example, how many laddoos were left unsold?
questions.explanation: 100 made − 25 sold = 75 laddoos left unsold.

questions.question: '80 children want samosas but the canteen only has 20' is an example of…
questions.explanation: 80 wanted but only 20 available means not enough to go around — a shortage.

questions.question: A seller prices her bangles so high that every customer walks away; they stay unsold and begin to rust. What was her mistake?
options: She set a price too high for buyers
She chose the wrong market to sell in
She did not bargain with customers
questions.explanation: Customers walking away is the sign of a too-high price. The problem was the price, not the quantity or the market.

questions.question: What happened to the bangles that stayed unsold for weeks?
options: They were sold at a surplus
questions.explanation: The chapter says the unsold bangles began to rust — unsold goods can spoil or become useless.

questions.question: A cricket match ticket selling out in four minutes shows very high demand.
questions.explanation: Selling out in minutes means many people wanted tickets and there were not enough — high demand.

questions.question: Petrol prices rising because oil supply drops is an example of a surplus.
questions.explanation: A drop in supply pushing prices up is a SHORTAGE. A surplus is when supply is greater than demand.

questions.question: The bangle seller's story best shows which chapter lesson?
options: When supply rises, prices usually fall
Bargaining is used at weekly haats
When a price is too high, the buyer walks away
When a price is too low, both lose in the end
questions.explanation: Her bangles stayed unsold and rusted because the price was too high and buyers walked away — the 'too high' case from the fair price section.

questions.question: Why is 'price will stay the same because supply has not changed' WRONG for the Sports Day samosas?
options: Supply of samosas actually fell on Sports Day
The canteen uncle gave the samosas away free
Prices in a canteen can never change
Price depends on demand too, and demand rose
questions.explanation: Price is decided by the balance of supply AND demand. Demand tripled, so even with the same supply the price rises.

questions.question: Which TWO scenarios show HIGH DEMAND?
options: 90 children want samosas on Sports Day
A cricket ticket sells out in four minutes
questions.explanation: Many children wanting samosas and a fast sell-out show high demand. Unsold laddoos and bangles show low demand for the price offered.

questions.question: How much did Kreena spend making her lemonade?
questions.explanation: Kreena spent ₹100 making lemonade (her expenditure). She earned ₹180 and made ₹80 profit.

questions.question: Which seller in the chapter had a clearly worked-out profit of ₹80?
questions.explanation: Kreena earned ₹180 from 30 cups at ₹6 and spent ₹100, a profit of ₹80. Myra's ₹90 is her income before costs.

questions.question: Which review scenario shows a seller losing because of PRICE rather than quantity?
options: A ticket sells out in four minutes
Bangles priced so high that nobody buys
questions.explanation: The bangle seller's problem was the price itself. The laddoos were a quantity surplus and the samosas a quantity shortage.

questions.question: Where does the chapter ask you to complete the L1 and L2 worksheets?
questions.explanation: The chapter says: 'Complete the L1 and L2 worksheets on Argus.'

questions.question: In the Connect project, what record of your learning do you build by adding each finished task?
questions.explanation: As you finish each task you add your work to the Portfolio, creating a record of your learning journey.

questions.question: Which portfolio task keeps track of pocket money, spending and savings?
questions.explanation: Count It: keep track of your pocket money, spending, savings and transactions.

questions.question: Which portfolio task analyses a local vendor scenario to understand profit, loss and break-even?
questions.explanation: Balance It: analyse a marketplace (local vendor) scenario to understand profit, loss and break-even through real-world calculations.

questions.question: Which portfolio task uses coordinates to locate and plot newly formed states on India's map?
questions.explanation: Map It: investigate India's changing map and use coordinates to locate and plot newly formed states.

questions.question: The Connect project says learning becomes more meaningful when applied to real-life situations.
questions.explanation: The Connect section opens with exactly this idea before listing the portfolio tasks.

questions.question: In the Balance It task, 'break-even' most likely means…
options: Income equals expenditure, no profit or loss
Income is far more than expenditure
Expenditure is far more than income
Supply is exactly equal to demand
questions.explanation: Break-even sits between profit and loss: the seller's income just covers costs, so there is no profit and no loss.

questions.question: Which TWO are portfolio tasks named in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The three portfolio tasks are Map It, Count It and Balance It.

questions.question: The Balance It task is about plotting newly formed states on a map.
questions.explanation: Plotting states is Map It. Balance It is about profit, loss and break-even for a local vendor.

questions.question: The chapter opens by asking 'Which version would you choose, and what would you have to give up for it?' This question is about…
options: Making a choice and what it costs you
Counting the tonnes at a mandi
Finding the highest bidder for a player
questions.explanation: Choosing one version means giving something up for it — every market choice has a cost.

questions.question: Which chapter number does the book give 'Markets and Trade: Where Buying Meets Selling'?
questions.explanation: The chapter opener shows 'Chapter 7 — Markets And Trade: Where Buying Meets Selling'.

questions.question: Checkpoint 2 asks you to draw arrows to show…
options: Which market makes the most sense
What happens to supply and price
questions.explanation: Checkpoint 2.1 says: read each story and draw arrows to show what will probably happen to the supply and the price.

questions.question: Checkpoint 1 asks you to decide which market makes the most sense for each situation.
questions.explanation: Checkpoint 1: read each situation carefully, decide which market makes the most sense, and give a reason why.

questions.question: Checkpoint 2 also asks you to tick whether each example describes a…
questions.explanation: Checkpoint 2.2 says: read each example and tick if it describes a shortage or a surplus.
